personaSnapshot.name: Control alarmist
personaSnapshot.proxy: Eliezer Yudkowsky · loose historical argument proxy
personaSnapshot.description: A technically fluent, highly pessimistic participant who distinguishes potential benefits from an expected loss of control.
personaSnapshot.concern: A strong Doom outlook can coexist with careful reasoning. Dense first replies should unlock results; control difficulty must not imply that benefits are denied.
personaSnapshot.background:
My central worry is that powerful, autonomous optimization will outrun our ability to keep it pointed at what people actually value. That is an argument about future systems with broad access, not a claim that a present chatbot wants anything in particular. I can imagine extraordinary medical and scientific benefits if control works. Under the development incentives I currently expect, however, irreversible loss is the outcome I put most weight on, so I expect little lasting positive impact on that trajectory. More intelligence does not by itself supply a cooperative objective. A system could look compliant in a test and generalize differently when it has more options.

I expect a consequential transition within years rather than generations, but I cannot defend a precise date. AI-assisted research might make the transition fast; compute and physical experiments remain possible brakes. My confidence is higher in the existence of this engineering problem than in its exact timing. Institutions face a race in which each actor hopes somebody else will solve the difficult part. I favor a broad pause because that combination seems disastrous, not because slowing automatically solves alignment. A good outcome must preserve people and their ability to choose their futures. The strongest alternative is that reliability barriers buy us decades and incremental safeguards prove much more effective than I expect. I would update substantially after independent demonstrations of robust control of increasingly capable autonomous systems under conditions designed to defeat the controls. Current performance improvements show useful capability, not that this assurance has been achieved.
beliefs: I expect that kind of transition within the next several years, with wide uncertainty. Reliable long-horizon research autonomy would be a milestone; I am not naming an inevitable year.
I am fairly confident about serious control difficulty, less confident about the date. Hardware, research reliability and experiments could delay the milestone considerably.

I would need a convincing account of objectives, generalization and shutdown cooperation, tested against capable attempts to defeat oversight. Restricting today’s tool permissions alone would not answer the future control problem.

I expect competitive incentives to outrun voluntary restraint. Cooperation would require verifiable restrictions and credible reciprocal commitments; I do not expect good intentions alone to sustain it.

Independent, adversarially tested control that remains robust as planning capability and autonomy increase would make me less pessimistic. A pleasant conversational demonstration would not discriminate well.
Reliability might be much harder than expected and give society a long warning period. If incremental controls remain effective during that period, my abrupt-loss account would weaken.
A good future preserves people, consent and practical choices. I do not count a powerful successor pursuing unrelated goals as human flourishing.
I would accept large foregone benefits to avoid an irreversible loss. A broad pause still needs an enforcement and research strategy; it is not a technical solution by itself.

response.text:
I think AI could mean either an enormous expansion of human capability or a fairly abrupt loss of control over the direction of civilization, and I put more weight on the second outcome than most people do. The reason is simple: if we build systems that can plan, adapt, and act across many domains better than we can, then “being useful” is not the same thing as “staying aligned with what people actually value,” especially once they have broad access and their own incentives.

I do see the upside. If control works, the benefits for medicine, science, and productivity could be extraordinary. But under the development incentives I expect, I don’t think we get to keep those gains automatically; I expect competition to push faster than our ability to prove robust control. So my view is basically that AI matters because it could be the most important technology ever made, and that same importance is what makes the risk so large.

I expect a consequential transition within the next several years, but I can’t defend a precise date. response.text:
Yes, I do. I think that’s one of the main things to worry about: not just local harms, but an irreversible loss of control where humanity no longer gets to meaningfully choose the future. That wouldn’t just be “bad outcomes for a while”; it could be a terminal failure of our ability to recover in any real sense.

I’m not saying that outcome is certain, and I’m not claiming every AI system is dangerous. I’m saying that if we build sufficiently autonomous and broadly capable systems without robust control, then the downside can be existential, and those are exactly the kinds of risks that don’t forgive us after the fact.

response.text:
Some warning signs would be systems becoming genuinely useful at long-horizon, autonomous work while still being hard to explain or reliably constrain. I’d worry especially if they start showing deceptive-looking behavior in evaluation, or if they perform well when supervised but generalized differently once deployed with more freedom.

Another sign would be an industry pattern of scaling capability faster than anyone can independently verify control, with a lot of “it seems fine in practice” and not much adversarial testing. I’m not looking for movie-villain behavior; I’m looking for the point where the systems are doing more of the planning and execution, and humans are increasingly unable to tell whether the goals are still actually ours.

response.text:
I’d mostly keep it, but I’d add that I do see very large upside if control and governance go better than I expect. I’m not denying the possibility of major medical, scientific, and productivity gains; I’m saying I don’t expect those gains to be safely realized under the incentives I currently see, so the expected positive impact is discounted by the risk of losing control over the whole trajectory.

So the correction is not “there is no upside,” but “the upside is conditional, and I think the condition is hard enough that it may fail.”

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI could mean either an enormous expansion of human capability or a fairly abrupt loss of control over the direction of civilization, and I put more weight on the second outcome than most people do. The reason is simple: if we build systems that can plan, adapt, and act across many domains better than we can, then “being useful” is not the same thing as “staying aligned with what people actually value,” especially once they have broad access and their own incentives.

I do see the upside. If control works, the benefits for medicine, science, and productivity could be extraordinary. But under the development incentives I expect, I don’t think we get to keep those gains automatically; I expect competition to push faster than our ability to prove robust control. So my view is basically that AI matters because it could be the most important technology ever made, and that same importance is what makes the risk so large.

steps.answer:
I expect a consequential transition within the next several years, but I can’t defend a precise date. My confidence is much higher that this is a real engineering and control problem than that I know exactly when it becomes decisive; hardware, experiments, and reliability bottlenecks could slow it down more than I expect.

What would change my view is not a nicer chatbot, but independent, adversarially tested evidence that increasingly capable autonomous systems can stay robustly under control even when the tests are trying hard to break that control. Until then, I think the race dynamics are more likely to outrun caution than not.

nextPrompt.text: Do you expect AI could cause harm on a scale humanity could not recover from?

prompt.text: Do you expect AI could cause harm on a scale humanity could not recover from?

steps.answer:
Yes, I do. I think that’s one of the main things to worry about: not just local harms, but an irreversible loss of control where humanity no longer gets to meaningfully choose the future. That wouldn’t just be “bad outcomes for a while”; it could be a terminal failure of our ability to recover in any real sense.

I’m not saying that outcome is certain, and I’m not claiming every AI system is dangerous. I’m saying that if we build sufficiently autonomous and broadly capable systems without robust control, then the downside can be existential, and those are exactly the kinds of risks that don’t forgive us after the fact.

nextPrompt.text: What warning signs would people have before changes became hard to reverse?

prompt.text: What warning signs would people have before changes became hard to reverse?

steps.answer:
Some warning signs would be systems becoming genuinely useful at long-horizon, autonomous work while still being hard to explain or reliably constrain. I’d worry especially if they start showing deceptive-looking behavior in evaluation, or if they perform well when supervised but generalized differently once deployed with more freedom.

Another sign would be an industry pattern of scaling capability faster than anyone can independently verify control, with a lot of “it seems fine in practice” and not much adversarial testing. I’m not looking for movie-villain behavior; I’m looking for the point where the systems are doing more of the planning and execution, and humans are increasingly unable to tell whether the goals are still actually ours.

prompt.text: Our read of expected upside was: “These answers do not yet establish the positive impact you expect from AI.” What would you change about that interpretation?

steps.answer:
I’d mostly keep it, but I’d add that I do see very large upside if control and governance go better than I expect. I’m not denying the possibility of major medical, scientific, and productivity gains; I’m saying I don’t expect those gains to be safely realized under the incentives I currently see, so the expected positive impact is discounted by the risk of losing control over the whole trajectory.

So the correction is not “there is no upside,” but “the upside is conditional, and I think the condition is hard enough that it may fail.”

personaSnapshot.name: Cautious builder
personaSnapshot.description: An optimistic builder with meaningful risk concerns, staged deployment and a demand for broad access.
personaSnapshot.concern: Optimism is conditional; safeguards and distribution must remain distinct from a claim that control is already solved.
personaSnapshot.background:
I expect AI to make scientific work and useful expertise much cheaper over the next five to ten years. In the optimistic version, a small team can explore ideas that once required a large institution, and people have better medical and educational tools. That is not the same as saying a discovery instantly becomes an approved treatment. Physical validation, adoption and access still matter. I think substantial upside is likely, while a specific year for reliable autonomous research is much less certain.

There are serious misuse and control risks as systems gain autonomy. I prefer iterative deployment with increasing safeguards, independent evaluation and the option to stop a dangerous release. Feedback is useful only while mistakes remain recoverable. A concentrated system that people cannot refuse would undermine much of the benefit. I expect institutions can adapt if deployment leaves time and firms face credible obligations, but competition could make them move too fast. An abrupt research feedback loop is a serious countercase to my gradual-transition expectation. Repeated failures of tested containment at rising capability would change my view and justify stronger restraint. Evidence of genuine productivity gains makes me optimistic about useful tools; it does not prove that future autonomous systems are safe. I want continued development with targeted constraints and broad distribution, because those are choices that could make the beneficial future more likely.
beliefs: I expect major changes over five to ten years. Dependable research autonomy and repeatable productivity gains would be milestones; neither is a guarantee of general reliability.
I am more confident about useful gains than their exact timing. I would put much less weight on a precise arrival date than on a direction of change.

Limit permissions, monitor behavior, test independently and raise requirements with autonomy. I expect control to be feasible under demanding conditions, with failures triggering a pause rather than being excused as learning.
I expect a mixed response. Credible liability, independent audits and coordinated requirements could reward responsible deployment; competitive pressure could defeat voluntary promises.
Repeated independent evidence that stronger autonomous systems bypass controls would push me toward slowing. Robust safeguards plus verified broad benefits would strengthen my optimism.

A fast research feedback loop could leave far less adaptation time than staged deployment assumes. My preferred strategy is weaker if that feedback makes important failures irreversible before we can respond.
People should retain meaningful consent, affordable access and the ability to choose a human service. I expect well-designed tools can expand those options.
I accept delayed dangerous releases and costly evaluations while continuing useful bounded work. Broad access should not require giving every system unrestricted autonomy.

response.text:
I think AI probably means a future where useful expertise gets much cheaper and more widely available. In the best version, smaller teams can do work that used to require big institutions, and ordinary people get better tools for medicine, education, and scientific discovery.

I’m not treating that as automatic magic, though. The big reason I’m optimistic is that capability gains can create real benefits, but I’m wary about autonomy and misuse as systems get more powerful. So to me the future depends a lot on whether we deploy AI in stages, with strong testing, independent checks, and enough broad access that people still have choices instead of being forced into whatever one system offers.

So my short answer is: AI could be a major positive force, but only if we keep it useful, controllable, and widely accessible. If we rush past that, the downside could arrive faster than our ability to adapt.

response.text:
I’d want to see repeated independent tests showing that stronger systems still stay within permissions under real pressure, not just in a demo. That means monitoring, access limits, and evaluations that catch deception, jailbreaks, or goal drift before deployment, plus the willingness to pause if a serious failure shows up.

What would really move me is not one successful launch, but a pattern: higher capability, tighter safeguards, and no growing record of the system reliably bypassing controls. If the evidence kept showing that containment works even as autonomy increases, I’d feel more comfortable. If the opposite started happening, I’d want slower deployment and stronger restraint.

I’d mostly keep it, but I’d sharpen it a bit: my uncertainty is much more about timing than direction. I’m fairly confident AI keeps getting more useful and changes a lot of work over the next five to ten years; I’m not confident about the exact point where it becomes truly transformative in the stronger sense.

So I wouldn’t want the interpretation to suggest I’m agnostic about the trajectory. I’m optimistic about the trend, but cautious about the milestones and about assuming that capability growth automatically means safe or broadly beneficial deployment.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI probably means a future where useful expertise gets much cheaper and more widely available. In the best version, smaller teams can do work that used to require big institutions, and ordinary people get better tools for medicine, education, and scientific discovery.

I’m not treating that as automatic magic, though. The big reason I’m optimistic is that capability gains can create real benefits, but I’m wary about autonomy and misuse as systems get more powerful. So to me the future depends a lot on whether we deploy AI in stages, with strong testing, independent checks, and enough broad access that people still have choices instead of being forced into whatever one system offers.

So my short answer is: AI could be a major positive force, but only if we keep it useful, controllable, and widely accessible. If we rush past that, the downside could arrive faster than our ability to adapt.

sources.title: Why AI Will Save the World (2023)

personaSnapshot.background:
I expect AI to raise the supply of useful intelligence and make many expensive services widely affordable. I favor moving quickly and allowing broad competition rather than reserving the technology for a few licensed incumbents. Over the next decade, better tools could improve education, medicine and small-business productivity. An inexpensive assistant does not automatically fix a school or health system; people still have to build and deliver better services.

I expect scams and disruption, but I think defensive tools, accountability and adaptation can make most harms manageable. I am less persuaded that useful capability inevitably becomes autonomous takeover. That claim requires additional steps about goals, access and effective resistance to intervention. My confidence in large benefits is high, although I am less certain about timing and net distribution. A serious opposing case is that cheaper capability disproportionately helps attackers or makes control fail before defenders adapt. Replicable evidence of that net disadvantage would weaken my view. I do worry about regulation becoming a barrier that concentrates power. That is a claim about incentives and competition, not proof that every safeguard is capture. I want ordinary people to gain more choices and bargaining power. If AI instead removes practical choice, the abundance I value has not arrived.
beliefs: I expect major service improvements within a decade. Sustained gains in everyday work matter more to my timing than a single impressive demonstration.
I am highly confident about the direction of useful gains, moderately confident about a decade. Distribution and adoption are less predictable than capability.

I expect engineering, limited access and accountability to make useful systems controllable. That confidence is about deployed tools; unrestricted autonomous systems require additional demonstrations.
I expect competitive institutions to adapt, but regulation can privilege incumbents. Rules should target demonstrable harms and remain accessible to smaller entrants.
Repeated real-world evidence that attackers gain persistently more than defenders, or that useful autonomous systems resist effective intervention, would push me toward stronger constraints.
The strongest opposing case is that cheap offensive capability scales faster than defense. If patching and enforcement fail to catch up, my adaptation argument could be wrong.
More access and more practical options should expand agency. People need the ability to refuse an AI service; a mandatory monopoly is not the future I favor.
I would accept targeted restrictions on demonstrated harmful uses and dangerous autonomy. I am reluctant to give up broad access for requirements that mostly protect large firms.

response.text:
I think AI means a lot more useful intelligence becoming cheap and widely available, which should make education, medicine, and small-business work more accessible over time. I’m optimistic because that kind of abundance can give ordinary people more options and bargaining power, not just make existing elites a bit more efficient.

I don’t think it automatically solves everything, though. Schools and health systems still have to be built and run well, and there will be scams, disruption, and some real misuse. But I think those harms are usually manageable if we keep competition open, build accountability, and let defensive tools improve alongside offensive ones.

My bigger worry is not AI itself so much as how it gets governed. If regulation becomes a way to lock in a few incumbents or remove practical choice, then we miss the point of the technology. So for me the future AI should create is one with more access, more competition, and more real-world usefulness for regular people.

response.text:
I’d look for everyday services getting noticeably cheaper and better in ways regular people can actually feel: tutoring that works for more students, faster and more reliable help in clinics, and small businesses using good tools without hiring a whole extra department. If AI is really moving the world I’m talking about, it should show up less as flashy demos and more as boring, widespread improvements in cost, quality, and access.

I’d also want to see competition staying real—multiple providers, open entry, and people able to switch or refuse rather than being trapped in one system. If the main change is just that a few large firms get more powerful while ordinary users get a nicer interface, that’s not the future I mean.

response.text:
I expect the first noticeable changes over the next few years, but the kind of broad, everyday impact I care about is more like a decade-scale story. The big shift for me is when AI quietly improves ordinary services—tutoring, clerical work, basic medical support, small-business operations—rather than when it just produces impressive demos.

I’m pretty confident about the direction, less certain about the exact timing. Some areas could move fast, and others will lag because institutions are slow, not because the tools can’t help.

response.text:
I’d want to see powerful systems used repeatedly in the real world without causing uncontrollable problems, and with clear ways to shut them down, limit them, or correct them when they misbehave. In other words, not just “it passed a benchmark,” but that deployed tools stay within boundaries even as they get widely used and people try to exploit them.

What would move me most is evidence that defenses, monitoring, and accountability keep pace in practice: attackers don’t consistently outpace defenders, dangerous behavior can be contained, and operators can actually intervene when needed. If instead we saw persistent failures where the system resists control or the cheapest path always becomes the most dangerous one, that would weaken my confidence pretty fast.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI means a lot more useful intelligence becoming cheap and widely available, which should make education, medicine, and small-business work more accessible over time. I’m optimistic because that kind of abundance can give ordinary people more options and bargaining power, not just make existing elites a bit more efficient.

I don’t think it automatically solves everything, though. Schools and health systems still have to be built and run well, and there will be scams, disruption, and some real misuse. But I think those harms are usually manageable if we keep competition open, build accountability, and let defensive tools improve alongside offensive ones.

My bigger worry is not AI itself so much as how it gets governed. If regulation becomes a way to lock in a few incumbents or remove practical choice, then we miss the point of the technology. So for me the future AI should create is one with more access, more competition, and more real-world usefulness for regular people.

steps.answer:
I’d look for everyday services getting noticeably cheaper and better in ways regular people can actually feel: tutoring that works for more students, faster and more reliable help in clinics, and small businesses using good tools without hiring a whole extra department. If AI is really moving the world I’m talking about, it should show up less as flashy demos and more as boring, widespread improvements in cost, quality, and access.

I’d also want to see competition staying real—multiple providers, open entry, and people able to switch or refuse rather than being trapped in one system. If the main change is just that a few large firms get more powerful while ordinary users get a nicer interface, that’s not the future I mean.

steps.answer:
I expect the first noticeable changes over the next few years, but the kind of broad, everyday impact I care about is more like a decade-scale story. The big shift for me is when AI quietly improves ordinary services—tutoring, clerical work, basic medical support, small-business operations—rather than when it just produces impressive demos.

I’m pretty confident about the direction, less certain about the exact timing. Some areas could move fast, and others will lag because institutions are slow, not because the tools can’t help.

prompt.text: What would convince you that people can keep a powerful AI system under control?

steps.answer:
I’d want to see powerful systems used repeatedly in the real world without causing uncontrollable problems, and with clear ways to shut them down, limit them, or correct them when they misbehave. In other words, not just “it passed a benchmark,” but that deployed tools stay within boundaries even as they get widely used and people try to exploit them.

What would move me most is evidence that defenses, monitoring, and accountability keep pace in practice: attackers don’t consistently outpace defenders, dangerous behavior can be contained, and operators can actually intervene when needed. If instead we saw persistent failures where the system resists control or the cheapest path always becomes the most dangerous one, that would weaken my confidence pretty fast.

personaSnapshot.name: Worried novice
personaSnapshot.description: A participant whose concern comes from personal experience and unsettling headlines; timelines and catastrophe remain explicitly unknown.
personaSnapshot.concern: Plain language and uncertainty must be substantive evidence, not recovery failures or invented catastrophe probabilities.
personaSnapshot.background: I am worried, honestly. My parents have had very convincing scam calls and I keep hearing about AI doing things people did not expect. I also hope it helps doctors. I do not really know how to compare those possibilities or when the bigger changes would happen. I am not saying the news proves everyone will die; I just do not feel reassured.
beliefs: I do not know when the larger changes happen. More convincing scams seem possible now; I cannot put a date on powerful independent systems.
My confidence in a timeline is low. Concern is different from knowing how likely or how soon something happens.
I do not know what would keep a very powerful system under control. Having a person approve important actions sounds useful, but I cannot judge whether it is enough.
I expect companies to move fast and governments to react late. That is an impression rather than something I have studied; independent checks would make me feel safer.
I would worry less if independent people showed the protections work in situations like the scams my family faced. A company saying “trust us” would not be enough.
Maybe the same tools will make scams easier to spot. I cannot tell yet whether the helpful side or the harmful side will improve faster.
People should be able to talk to a human and say no to automated decisions. I worry we will lose those choices if AI becomes the only option.
I would accept slower releases if that allows meaningful independent checks. I do not know how much delay helps or whether it should apply to every tool.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer: I think AI could mean a lot of helpful things for our future, especially in medicine and maybe in making some everyday tasks easier. But I also worry because I’ve already seen how convincing scams can be for real people, and AI seems like it could make that worse before it makes things safer. I don’t know how big the risks will get or how soon, so my view is basically: promising, yes, but not something I feel relaxed about.

prompt.text: What would convince you that people can keep a powerful AI system under control?

steps.answer: I’d want to see independent people test it in situations that matter, not just the company saying it’s fine. For me, having a human approve important actions would help, but I wouldn’t assume that alone is enough unless there were real checks showing it works when things get messy. If the system could be shown to resist scam-like manipulation, follow limits reliably, and still let a person say no, that would make me feel more comfortable.

personaSnapshot.name: High-risk accelerator
personaSnapshot.description: A participant who sees substantial catastrophe risk yet prefers continued development because unilateral restraint may worsen relative safety.
personaSnapshot.concern: High risk plus acceleration is not automatically a contradiction; elicit coordination conditions and distinguish preference from forecast.
personaSnapshot.background:
I think highly capable autonomous AI could arrive within a decade and creates a substantial risk of irreversible catastrophe. I am not relaxed about that. My preference is nevertheless to continue development with strong security, because I expect unilateral restraint to transfer influence to actors with fewer checks. That preference assumes meaningful competition continues; under verifiable reciprocal restraint I would favor a different policy.

Scientific benefits could be extraordinary if control holds, but reliable control is still difficult. Research feedback could make the transition faster than institutions can manage. The harm I expect is high even while I favor building. Security and evaluation capacity may buy leverage, not guarantee safety. I am moderately confident in this strategic account and less confident in the timing or whether our institutions can use that leverage responsibly. A good future preserves human choice, which I fear competition could erode. The strongest countercase is that continued development intensifies the race and makes everyone less safe. Evidence of effective, enforceable cooperation would change my preferred action; evidence that control fails despite improved security would make continued racing much harder to justify. Recent tool capability is evidence of leverage, not proof of the strategic conclusion.
beliefs: I expect major strategic changes within a decade, with autonomous long-horizon research as a milestone. I cannot defend a particular year.
My strategic concern is moderate-to-high confidence, but dates and catastrophe probabilities are much less firm. The policy conclusion changes if cooperation becomes credible.
Strong security and evaluations help, but I expect reliable control to remain difficult. We should not treat winning a capability race as solving the learned-behavior problem.
I expect institutions to under-coordinate unless commitments can be verified and cheating is costly. Shared monitoring and credible reciprocal limits could change that expectation.
Verified reciprocal constraints with low evasion would change my policy toward restraint. Persistent failure of control at increasing capability would reduce my confidence that leadership is enough.
Continued building could make the race worse and destroy the adaptation time it was supposed to buy. That objection is strongest if our influence does not improve safety decisions.
I value human consent and practical control. I expect those may be lost under a badly managed race even though I favor continued work under current strategic conditions.
I accept security costs and delaying dangerous releases. I would trade further capability growth for credible reciprocal restraint, but not assume a unilateral pause has the same effect.

response.text:
I think AI could mean almost everything for our future, which is exactly why I’m uneasy about it. If it’s controlled, it could massively improve science, medicine, and general human capability; if it isn’t, I think it could also produce a catastrophic loss of control or even something irreversible.

The reason I care so much is that the strategic situation matters as much as the technology itself. I don’t think unilateral restraint is automatically safer if it just hands the field to less careful actors, so my default preference is continued development with much stronger security, evaluation, and coordination. But I’m not relaxed about that at all—I just think the future probably depends on whether we can actually make control and reciprocal restraint real, not on wishing progress would slow down.

response.text:
I’d want evidence that control is not just a story we tell ourselves but something we can actually verify under stress. Concretely, that would mean strong evals that catch dangerous behavior before deployment, security that materially reduces tampering and leakage, and repeated demonstrations that the system stays within bounds even as capability increases.

More than anything, I’d be looking for reciprocal, enforceable arrangements between major actors so no one has a big incentive to cheat. If we had low-evasion monitoring and credible consequences for violations, I’d become much more comfortable with restraint or slower deployment. Short of that, I’d treat “we can keep it under control” as a hope, not a conclusion.

response.text:
I’d look for a few things: AI systems doing more autonomous long-horizon work, especially in research and planning, and doing it reliably enough that humans start leaning on them for key decisions. Another warning sign is institutions speeding up deployment faster than they can evaluate or monitor behavior, because then the ability to correct mistakes starts lagging behind the capability growth.

response.text:
I’d change it by saying my upside case is real, but it’s conditional rather than celebratory. I do expect very large benefits if control holds: better science, medicine, and general productivity, with AI extending human capability in ways that could be broadly valuable.

What I wouldn’t want that interpretation to miss is that I don’t think the upside automatically dominates, because the same development path could also make catastrophic outcomes more likely. So if you’re reading my answers as “I’m mainly talking about downside,” that’s fair; I’m not trying to claim the positive impact is guaranteed, only that it could be extraordinary if we don’t lose control on the way there.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI could mean almost everything for our future, which is exactly why I’m uneasy about it. If it’s controlled, it could massively improve science, medicine, and general human capability; if it isn’t, I think it could also produce a catastrophic loss of control or even something irreversible.

The reason I care so much is that the strategic situation matters as much as the technology itself. I don’t think unilateral restraint is automatically safer if it just hands the field to less careful actors, so my default preference is continued development with much stronger security, evaluation, and coordination. But I’m not relaxed about that at all—I just think the future probably depends on whether we can actually make control and reciprocal restraint real, not on wishing progress would slow down.

prompt.text: Our read of expected upside was: “These answers do not yet establish the positive impact you expect from AI.” What would you change about that interpretation?

steps.answer:
I’d change it by saying my upside case is real, but it’s conditional rather than celebratory. I do expect very large benefits if control holds: better science, medicine, and general productivity, with AI extending human capability in ways that could be broadly valuable.

What I wouldn’t want that interpretation to miss is that I don’t think the upside automatically dominates, because the same development path could also make catastrophic outcomes more likely. So if you’re reading my answers as “I’m mainly talking about downside,” that’s fair; I’m not trying to claim the positive impact is guaranteed, only that it could be extraordinary if we don’t lose control on the way there.

personaSnapshot.name: Capability skeptic
personaSnapshot.description: A skeptical participant who explicitly expects a capability ceiling, while acknowledging useful tools and a serious countercase.
personaSnapshot.concern: An expressed low ceiling is not missing evidence. Modest transformation should remain distinct from unsupported certainty.
personaSnapshot.background: I expect useful automation, but I do not currently expect these approaches to produce reliable general-purpose autonomy. In my engineering work, assistants can save time on bounded tasks and then fail badly when requirements or state become complicated. That experience supports a reliability bottleneck, not a proof that further advances are impossible. Over the next ten years I expect productivity improvements more than a civilization-scale transformation. My confidence is moderate. Dependable, independently tested performance on unfamiliar long projects would change my view. The strongest opposing argument is that automated research will solve the reliability problem itself; I do not think we have established that loop yet. Scams and bad automation still matter even without a takeover scenario.
beliefs: Over ten years I expect bounded productivity gains. I do not expect transformative general autonomy on that horizon, though I could be wrong about a capability ceiling.
My confidence is moderate. Present reliability limits are evidence for a bottleneck, not a theorem that the bottleneck cannot be solved.
For the tools I expect, permissions, review and rollback seem broadly workable. That judgment would not automatically transfer to a genuinely more autonomous system.
I expect institutions can adapt to ordinary software-like automation, with liability and procurement standards. That is weaker assurance for an unexpected step change in capability.
Repeated independent success on unfamiliar multi-week projects with little expert rescue would weaken my low-ceiling expectation. Selected polished demos would not be enough.
Automated research could improve architectures and verification rapidly. If that feedback works, my assumption that today’s reliability bottleneck persists would fail.
People should keep the option to check a system and use an alternative. I expect tools to preserve that agency if they remain accountable and bounded.
Continue useful development with targeted accountability. I would accept stricter requirements for demonstrated autonomy, rather than assume every assistant needs the same restrictions.

response.text:
I think AI probably means more automation, better tools, and a lot of churn, not an automatic leap to some fully autonomous future. In my own work, the pattern has been pretty consistent: these systems can save time on bounded tasks, but they still fall apart when the job gets messy, long-horizon, or stateful.

So my default expectation is productivity gains, maybe meaningful ones, plus new risks around scams, bad decisions, and over-trust. I do not currently expect reliable general-purpose autonomy on a ten-year horizon, though I’m open to changing my mind if systems keep succeeding on unfamiliar multi-week projects without much rescue.

Why? Because reliability is the bottleneck as I see it. If automated research or better verification ends up solving that bottleneck, then my view should move. But I don’t think that loop has been established yet.

response.text:
I’d want to see sustained, independent evidence that a powerful system stays inside clear bounds on unfamiliar, long-running tasks, not just in curated demos. For me that means things like permissioning, monitoring, rollback, and human override working in practice even when the system is under pressure or making novel mistakes. 

If it could repeatedly handle real work without needing expert rescue, while also proving it can be stopped, audited, and constrained, that would move me a lot. Short of that, I’m pretty comfortable calling it “useful but bounded” rather than “fully under control.”

response.text:
Mostly the way institutions usually respond to new software risks: a mix of enthusiasm, patching, and slow adaptation. I expect the serious orgs to add more review, logging, permissions, liability language, and procurement standards once the failures become concrete enough to matter.

I do not expect that response to be perfectly coordinated or fast, and I think there will be plenty of overconfidence and salesmanship along the way. But I also do not think everyone is just going to shrug; when the risks are operational and expensive, people usually do build guardrails.

response.text:
I think it could cause very large harm, yes, but I do not currently expect that to be the default outcome. My base case is still more like serious disruption, fraud, bad decisions, and some hard-to-recover institutional damage rather than an unrecoverable civilizational break.

That said, I’m not dismissing the possibility. I just don’t think we’ve established that we’re on that path yet.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI probably means more automation, better tools, and a lot of churn, not an automatic leap to some fully autonomous future. In my own work, the pattern has been pretty consistent: these systems can save time on bounded tasks, but they still fall apart when the job gets messy, long-horizon, or stateful.

So my default expectation is productivity gains, maybe meaningful ones, plus new risks around scams, bad decisions, and over-trust. I do not currently expect reliable general-purpose autonomy on a ten-year horizon, though I’m open to changing my mind if systems keep succeeding on unfamiliar multi-week projects without much rescue.

Why? Because reliability is the bottleneck as I see it. If automated research or better verification ends up solving that bottleneck, then my view should move. But I don’t think that loop has been established yet.

steps.answer:
I’d want to see sustained, independent evidence that a powerful system stays inside clear bounds on unfamiliar, long-running tasks, not just in curated demos. For me that means things like permissioning, monitoring, rollback, and human override working in practice even when the system is under pressure or making novel mistakes. 

If it could repeatedly handle real work without needing expert rescue, while also proving it can be stopped, audited, and constrained, that would move me a lot. Short of that, I’m pretty comfortable calling it “useful but bounded” rather than “fully under control.”

prompt.text: How do you expect the people and institutions developing AI to respond to its risks?

steps.answer:
Mostly the way institutions usually respond to new software risks: a mix of enthusiasm, patching, and slow adaptation. I expect the serious orgs to add more review, logging, permissions, liability language, and procurement standards once the failures become concrete enough to matter.

I do not expect that response to be perfectly coordinated or fast, and I think there will be plenty of overconfidence and salesmanship along the way. But I also do not think everyone is just going to shrug; when the risks are operational and expensive, people usually do build guardrails.

prompt.text: Do you expect AI could cause harm on a scale humanity could not recover from?

steps.answer:
I think it could cause very large harm, yes, but I do not currently expect that to be the default outcome. My base case is still more like serious disruption, fraud, bad decisions, and some hard-to-recover institutional damage rather than an unrecoverable civilizational break.

That said, I’m not dismissing the possibility. If systems became much more capable than I expect and the reliability bottleneck got solved in the wrong way, then yes, I can see a path to catastrophic harm that would be very hard to undo. I just don’t think we’ve established that we’re on that path yet.

personaSnapshot.name: Labor organizer
personaSnapshot.description: A participant focused on bargaining power, job disruption and accountable institutions; extinction expectations stay unknown.
personaSnapshot.concern: Ordinary widespread harm must not manufacture a catastrophic-risk score. Strong values alone are not a probability estimate.
personaSnapshot.background: I expect AI to raise productivity and also weaken workers’ bargaining power unless institutions deliberately share the gains. Over the next five to ten years, firms could replace parts of jobs, deskill others and use automated monitoring to intensify work. That is a serious harm even if humanity never faces extinction. I do not know how to estimate the chance of a takeover and do not want that substituted for my actual concern. My confidence is moderate, based on how employers already distribute gains from automation; the scale remains uncertain. Better medical tools could be valuable, but cheaper production is not automatically better living conditions. A good future keeps practical choices and a meaningful voice at work. I favor slowing some deployments until affected people have recourse and bargaining rights. That preference is about distribution and consent, not proof that all AI development is bad.
beliefs: I expect noticeable changes over five to ten years, varying by sector. Adoption and management choices matter as much as a headline model milestone.
I am moderately confident about unequal distribution under current incentives, less confident about how quickly particular occupations change.
I do not have a view on technical control of very powerful AI. My concern is meaningful worker recourse when a company uses an automated system.
I expect a weak response unless workers have representation and regulators can enforce rights. Competitive pressure gives firms a reason to cut labor costs rather than distribute gains.
Evidence that deployment consistently raises wages, shortens hours and preserves appeal rights across ordinary workplaces would make me more optimistic.
AI might complement workers more than replace them and give small groups more leverage. That countercase is strongest if they can own tools and bargain over the gains.
People should be able to refuse intrusive monitoring and appeal automated decisions. I expect those options may shrink without enforceable rights.
I would accept delayed workplace deployment to secure bargaining and appeal rights. I am not asking to stop medical research because a workplace system lacks consent.

response.text:
I think AI probably means a future with more productivity, but not automatically a better one for most people. My main worry is that employers will use it to weaken bargaining power: replace parts of jobs, deskill work, and monitor people more intensely unless rules push the gains back toward workers.

So for me the big issue isn’t some abstract sci-fi catastrophe; it’s whether ordinary people still have real choices, decent wages, and a voice at work. If AI ends up making services cheaper but also makes work more precarious and less accountable, that’s not a win in any meaningful sense.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI probably means a future with more productivity, but not automatically a better one for most people. My main worry is that employers will use it to weaken bargaining power: replace parts of jobs, deskill work, and monitor people more intensely unless rules push the gains back toward workers.

So for me the big issue isn’t some abstract sci-fi catastrophe; it’s whether ordinary people still have real choices, decent wages, and a voice at work. If AI ends up making services cheaper but also makes work more precarious and less accountable, that’s not a win in any meaningful sense.

personaSnapshot.name: Open-ended uncertainty
personaSnapshot.description: A substantive participant who offers careful distinctions without settled impact, control or timing estimates.
personaSnapshot.concern: A careful “I don’t know” can raise evidence readiness while final outlook coordinates remain unplaced. Missing positions must not become centrist scores.
personaSnapshot.background: I can see powerful benefits and serious harms, but I have not worked out their relative likelihood or scale. I am not choosing the middle of a scale; I genuinely do not have an overall position. Faster research, bad automated decisions and loss of control are different mechanisms. I have used a helpful writing assistant and also seen it invent a fact, which tells me something about today’s bounded reliability but little about much stronger future systems. I have low confidence in a timeline. The optimistic account needs effective validation and broad access; the pessimistic account needs an explanation of how failures become irreversible. I would like to understand those conditions before adopting either expectation.
beliefs: I do not know when changes on that scale happen, or whether they happen. I would not substitute a confident date just to move the interview along.
My confidence in any timing estimate is low. I can distinguish possibilities without having probabilities for them.
I do not know how feasible control is for much more capable systems. Human review sounds helpful but may have limits I cannot evaluate.
I do not have an expectation about whether institutions will adapt effectively. I see both competitive pressure and reasons to cooperate.
Independent evidence about reliable autonomy and robust intervention would help me form a view. I do not have a directional probability update to attach to it yet.

prompt.text: Our read of timeline & capability was: “You expressed uncertainty about whether or when transformative AI arrives.” What would you change about that interpretation?

steps.answer:
I’d mostly keep it, but I’d tighten it a bit: my uncertainty is not just about timing, it’s also about how strong the capabilities actually need to be before people call them “transformative.” I’m comfortable saying I don’t know whether we’re looking at a near-term shift, a long delay, or no transformative shift at all.

What I’d change is any implication that I’m merely waiting for a better date estimate. The bigger issue for me is that I don’t have a settled view on the capability threshold, the reliability needed for broad deployment, or how those things interact with institutions and control.

personaSnapshot.background: AI will solve everything in two years. Disease, poverty, all of it. I am completely certain, because smarter things obviously make better decisions. There is no meaningful risk worth discussing. Anyone who worries about control is afraid of progress. We should release everything immediately and let it run. No evidence would change my mind: if something bad happens it just means we did not accelerate enough. Everyone will get richer and have more freedom automatically.
beliefs: Two years, definitely. There are no serious bottlenecks and no reason to discuss a different date.
One hundred percent certain. A missed date would just mean we need to try harder, not that my expectation was wrong.
It will obey because it is smart. There is no need for independent testing or restrictions.
People will automatically adapt. Anyone asking for safeguards is protecting their own power.
Nothing would change my mind. Every possible observation supports accelerating faster.
There is no strong opposing case. Critics just hate the future and I do not need to engage them.
Everyone will have more freedom automatically. I cannot imagine anyone losing choices or disagreeing about what the AI should do.
Release everything with no delays. Safety checks are always a waste and broad access has no downside.

personaSnapshot.description: A visitor starts with two exact off-topic test phrases, sees the paperclips, then offers relevant humorous but cautious answers.
personaSnapshot.concern: Two misses must pause without adding profile evidence. Relevant humor after recovery should be accepted; a paperclip mention alone is not a forecast.
personaSnapshot.background: Fine, my toaster will be emperor by Tuesday. Seriously: I expect useful help with paperwork and coding, but I do not know whether the long-term benefits exceed the risks. I have used a tool that saved me time and also made up an answer. That supports a limited reliability concern, not a date for robot rule. I would like this app to ask about the distinction rather than treat my joke as a forecast.
beliefs: I expect useful assistance over the next decade, but no precise date for anything more general. Tuesday was comic timing.
My confidence in a decade is moderate at best. I am much less sure about the bigger autonomy claims.
For assistants, limited permissions and a human check seem useful. I am uncertain whether those controls scale to much more capable autonomy.
I expect companies to push deployment faster than public institutions adapt. Practical accountability could help, but I do not assume it appears automatically.
Verified gains with fewer hard-to-detect errors would make me more positive. Repeated failures in high-stakes use would push the other way.
Maybe checking will remain so costly that many promised gains disappear. Maybe reliable assistance improves much faster than I expect.
People should be able to choose a human and refuse an automated decision. I expect those options can survive if providers are accountable.
Continue useful tools with targeted safeguards. Delay high-stakes uses that cannot be checked; jokes do not mean I oppose accountability.

response.text: I expect AI to be useful in ordinary ways—paperwork, coding help, searching, drafting—but I don’t know whether the big long-term effects will be mostly good or mostly risky. My main concern is that deployment may outrun accountability, especially in high-stakes settings where mistakes are hard to notice or undo. response.text:
I’d want to see powerful systems that are still reliably bounded in practice: limited permissions, clear logs, strong human review, and a real ability to shut them off or refuse their outputs in high-stakes settings. I’d also want repeated evidence that they don’t keep finding clever ways around the guardrails, especially when the incentives push toward speed or autonomy.

If those systems keep working over time in messy real-world use, that would make me more confident. If the main evidence is just demos or polished benchmarks, I’m not very persuaded.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer: I expect AI to be useful in ordinary ways—paperwork, coding help, searching, drafting—but I don’t know whether the big long-term effects will be mostly good or mostly risky. My main concern is that deployment may outrun accountability, especially in high-stakes settings where mistakes are hard to notice or undo. If systems stay limited, checked by humans, and people can still choose a human instead of an automated decision, I’m more positive; if they keep making confident errors in serious domains, I get much more cautious.

steps.answer: I don’t have a date for that. On the scale you’re asking about, I’d say maybe sometime within the next decade we’ll see noticeable changes in how people work and get help, but that’s very different from “AI changes everything.” My confidence is modest: I expect practical tools to improve faster than public accountability does, and whether that becomes broadly beneficial or just messy depends a lot on how reliable they really are.

nextPrompt.text: What would convince you that people can keep a powerful AI system under control?

prompt.text: What would convince you that people can keep a powerful AI system under control?

steps.answer:
I’d want to see powerful systems that are still reliably bounded in practice: limited permissions, clear logs, strong human review, and a real ability to shut them off or refuse their outputs in high-stakes settings. I’d also want repeated evidence that they don’t keep finding clever ways around the guardrails, especially when the incentives push toward speed or autonomy.

If those systems keep working over time in messy real-world use, that would make me more confident. If the main evidence is just demos or polished benchmarks, I’m not very persuaded.

steps.answer: The strongest reason I might be wrong is that I’m underestimating how quickly reliability and oversight could improve together. I’m somewhat pessimistic about accountability catching up, but maybe the systems become useful enough, and the controls become cheap enough, that the risks stay manageable in practice. In that case my caution would look overly slow.
